answers.q: Why should I hire you?
aliases: what makes you a good fit
why should we bring you on
answers.a: I get fluent in hard domains fast. Space traffic, health records, academic integrity, disaster response, government, systems engineering. Six of them, none of which I knew going in. I will understand the problem you are trying to solve as well as you do. And I prototype in code and ship my own front-end PRs, so what I hand you is the thing, not a picture of the thing.

answers.q: Three years without critique. Can you take feedback?
answers.a: I had formal critique at Turnitin for four years and group critique at Slingshot. I lost it at Sysgit and built my own design critique skill to stand in for it, rather than getting comfortable without it. I would rather be a designer who missed critique than one who learned to do without.

answers.q: Have you ever worked inside a real design org?
aliases: can you work with other designers
what size teams have you been on
have you worked with other designers
have you been on a big team
answers.a: Four years at Turnitin: twenty designers, formal process, and a design system I contributed to but did not own. I was also lead to three junior designers there. At Slingshot I was the only designer on Beacon but part of a company design team with shared critique. Sysgit is the only place I have been the entire design function.

answers.q: Have you led other designers?
answers.a: Yes. Lead to three junior designers at Turnitin, inside a twenty-person design org with formal process and critique.

answers.q: What do you want to be hired to do next?
aliases: what are you looking for in your next role
what kind of company do you want
where do you want to work
answers.a: A hard problem, and explicitly not necessarily systems engineering. Twice now I have found a standard-setting vacuum and not been able to fill it: interaction conventions for SysML v2 at Sysgit, and collision-avoidance procedure at Slingshot. So it is more specific than wanting a hard problem. I want somewhere I can set the standard, not only build inside one.

answers.q: What are you bad at?
aliases: where do you need to grow
what are you working on improving
answers.a: I am pretty trash at documentation and formal process. Way too much lives in my head at any given time, and I regularly ignore my own advice to others, which is never be afraid to state the obvious, because it is not obvious to everyone. This site is partly the correction. Writing it forced most of that out of my head and into a file.

answers.q: Where are your metrics?
aliases: what was the impact of your work
answers.a: Sysgit has no product analytics. That is a gap I own rather than defend. Beacon has two published adoption figures, both cited on its page with their denominators. Everywhere else I would rather show you the decision and the tradeoff than a number I cannot defend in a room.

answers.q: Why have you jumped between so many industries?
aliases: what industries have you worked in
what domains have you worked in
answers.a: I did not pick them for variety. Each one was a hard problem I did not already understand, and getting to competence fast is the actual skill. Space traffic, enterprise healthcare, academic integrity, disaster response, government, systems engineering. Six domains, none of which I knew going in.

answers.q: Do you actually write production code?
aliases: how much code do you ship
answers.a: Full features, not just copy and CSS. I avoid anything that would substantially touch the backend. The process is deliberately not shortened: a design review with a prototype handoff, then a formal PR review like anyone else. Having merge access never became a reason to skip review. My engineers were supportive early on, when I was making a lot of junior dev mistakes.

answers.q: Is this a chatbot?
aliases: am i talking to a bot
am i talking to a robot
am i talking to a human
answers.a: No. There is no model here. Every answer was written in advance and is being retrieved. There is no improvising. I've been a vocal chatbot hater for years and it would be hypocritical to start here.

answers.q: Did AI write this site?
aliases: did you use ai for this
answers.a: Partly, and it would honestly be weird if it hadn't, given that I claim it's integral to my process. I built it in VS Code with Claude Code. The interviews, the decisions about what to include, and every judgment call about what I can defend are mine. The model generates and summarizes, and I have final say and polish. That division is the same one I use at work.

answers.q: Are designers going to be replaced by AI?
aliases: are you worried about ai taking your job
answers.a: Generation is delegable; evaluation and taste are not. The part of my job a model does well is producing more options than I would have made alone, and the part it does badly is knowing which one is right for a user it has never met in a domain it has thin data on. I have not found that second part getting easier. I am also a much better personality hire.

answers.q: What will you not use AI for?
aliases: where do you draw the line
when do you not use ai
what do you do by hand
answers.a: Anything needing real subject matter expertise. I work in pretty niche fields and I cannot assume the training data is there. Use the model where coverage is dense, not where it is sparse. And UI review is always manual. I need to click around and find what feels clunky. Generation is delegable. Evaluation is not.

answers.q: Is AI native a buzzword, or do you mean something by it?
aliases: are you just a chatgpt wrapper
how do you use ai in your work
how does ai fit into your process
how much ai do you use
answers.a: To me, being AI native means it is an integral part of my design workflow, just as Figma was not too long ago. It has the same caveats: my job was never drawing boxes, any more than it is writing prompts. It's just a different material with which to do the same work. Being AI native also means fundamentally understanding where models weak, when to let them run wild, and having the expertise to know when they're wrong.

answers.q: How do you feel about AI?
aliases: what do you think about ai
what is your take on ai
how do you feel about machine learning
answers.a: As a designer it has been a game changer, because it opened code as a design medium. That is a gap Figma has been awkwardly trying to close for years. It also accelerates the backroom parts of creative work: brainstorming, finding inspiration. I am also deeply worried about the ethics of unrestrained models and recursive improvement. I have seen first-hand, in education and in healthcare, the human cost of leaning too hard on machine learning and taking a person out of the decision.

answers.q: When does AI belong in a product?
aliases: how do you decide where ai goes
when is ai the right call
should we put ai in our product
when not to use ai in a product
how do you evaluate ai features
answers.a: It has to pass one of two tests. Either it is solving a real time sink that is nobody's actual job, or it is standing in for a subject matter expert you cannot get in the room. If it is neither, nobody has demonstrated a need. I said no to chatbots at Sysgit for three years on exactly that basis.

answers.q: Do you still use Figma?
aliases: what design tools do you use
answers.a: Barely. I tried Figma Make and the Figma MCP when they launched and the results were never what I wanted. The useful realization was sharper than the tooling verdict: I was looking for reasons to justify continuing to use Figma. Designers are professionally defined by that tool. It is the same attachment Sysgit's users have to the software I am replacing.

answers.q: Why did you leave Slingshot?
aliases: why only a year at slingshot
why did you only stay a year
answers.a: Layoff for headcount reasons, Series A, 2023. About a year. Beacon's adoption at the time makes it fairly clear it was not a performance question.

answers.q: Do you do product, or just design?
answers.a: Both, twice, and not by choice the first time. At Slingshot there was no manager and no PM who lasted, so strategy happened jointly with the engineering manager. At Sysgit I report to the VP of Engineering and serve as part-time PM. Twice is a pattern: I fill the product strategy vacuum in engineering-led companies, because otherwise nobody does.

answers.q: What was the hardest thing to get right?
answers.a: The diagramming. In hardware modeling a square is not a square. It carries model metadata, and position and lines have specific meaning. The diagram also has to translate directly into the mental model of coded files, and back, for people who think visually and people who think in code. I designed toward the bare minimum required for an object to exist, and no further.

answers.q: What did you get wrong?
answers.a: The commenting system. I assumed collaboration needed a discussion layer and designed the whole workflow before questioning the premise. It was too convoluted to implement and users were ambivalent. The async version control model was already doing the collaboration work. I had designed a synchronous-feeling layer on top of an async system.

answers.q: Where were you overruled?
aliases: what were you not allowed to do
answers.a: The modeling vocabulary. My whole thesis is that this is a translation problem: picture, document, and code, legible to two cohorts. The words are the one layer I have not been allowed to translate, because the founder wants strict spec fidelity and the company will not take a position on the language. So the product translates every representation except the language itself.

answers.q: What have you said no to?
aliases: what did you push back on
answers.a: Chatbots, repeatedly. Nobody could demonstrate an actual need for one. Also one-off features requested for a demo or by a single prospective customer. The automated PM absorbs a lot of that pressure now, because a weighted ticket from real signal is harder to argue with than a designer saying no in a meeting.

answers.q: Who pushes back on you, and what happened last time?
answers.a: Engineers argue a design is more technically demanding than it looks. Founders argue it does not match their industry experience. Most recently an engineer built a proof of concept for a worker management activity. I tried repeatedly to reframe it as analogous to AI agent creation and could not get it across. We fixed it by sitting down and mapping the actual workflow, which should have happened before anyone touched code.

answers.q: How do you get access to systems engineers?
aliases: how did you talk to users
how much research did you do
answers.a: I stopped waiting for research to be scheduled and embedded myself in our RevOps process instead, so I am in the initial calls as the non-sales person in the room. Thirty-plus interviews that way. I also lurk in systems engineering Discord and Reddit, and I walk the floor at defense conferences I happen to be attending.

answers.q: What did being the only designer stop you from doing?
answers.a: Product design is ultimately a collaborative process, and the benefit of the design team is a group of people who already know the rules and the language. Solo designers have to find unique ways to get outside perspective and create their own feedback loop.

answers.q: Why are the Beacon screens recreations?
answers.a: I left Slingshot in 2023 and have no access to the product. Everything on this page is reconstructed from a couple of surviving Figma files and memory, and it is captioned that way. I would rather label a reconstruction than pass one off as a screenshot.

answers.q: What did you get wrong?
answers.a: I let the interface get ahead of the information architecture. There was a push from other product teams to make Beacon look especially cutting edge and I went along with it. In a product whose whole job is making dense, uneven data legible under time pressure, the structure was the thing worth polishing. I wish I had pushed back.

answers.q: How do you design something with no prior art?
answers.a: You anchor to the data, because it is the only thing that exists. Conjunction messages and ephemerides are extremely dense, so I printed them and had subject matter experts circle exactly what they looked at during real decision points. That is the opposite of Sysgit, where there is an incumbent and I designed toward what users were already trained on.

answers.q: How did you get operators to share data they did not have to share?
answers.a: Position is not the sensitive part. Capability is. Ground sensor networks see your assets whether you like it or not, so sharing position helps everyone. What operators actually guard is their risk thresholds and whether an asset can maneuver at all. I built those as optional signals rather than requirements, and operators got more willing to share once they could see what others had shared in turn. Beacon ended up more trusted than the public catalog it sat alongside.

answers.q: What is still unsolved?
answers.a: Operators asked constantly: what should we do, what should our standard operating procedure be. For most of them this was a genuinely new discipline with no established practice to follow. Slingshot was in a unique position to set that standard and did not. I still think about it.

answers.q: Is this the AI writing detector?
aliases: did you build the ai detector
answers.a: No. This was contract cheating: human ghostwriters, shipped in 2019. In 2018 AI was nowhere near mature enough to be the problem. Machine learning was the backbone of contract cheating detection, so the ML framing is accurate. Turnitin does now sell an AI writing detection product. I did not work on it.

answers.q: What did you get wrong?
answers.a: I made the product prescriptive first, using the phrase Investigation Recommended. Research found educators still read it as an accusation, which was the exact thing I was trying to design away from. I backed the severity down and moved to more nuanced signals that bring a piece of work to a teacher's attention rather than pronouncing on it.

answers.q: What made this harder than it looks?
answers.a: Two things. Legally the product could not say a student had cheated, so it had to surface suspicious factors across a body of work instead. And Turnitin's flagship Similarity product already had a reputation for being wrong and over-trusted, with students publicly describing unfair accusations. I was designing against my own company's history of producing scores people believed too much.

answers.q: What happened when the research contradicted what the company sold?
aliases: why is the model not first
how did you handle the company line
answers.a: Research kept turning up the same thing: file metadata caught more cheating than the model did. Author name, editing time, dates that did not match. So I moved those to the top of the report and put the linguistic analysis below them. Leadership did not want the model demoted and we settled on a split. Sales kept leading with the machine learning. The product showed whatever actually made the case.

answers.q: Why include a project that did not work?
answers.a: Because it covers two things nothing else does: mobile, and working alongside another designer. And it taught me the thing I use most. You inherit blame for user error that your own friction caused. A student rushing a tedious mapping step at midnight produces a bad submission, and the teacher blames the product. The friction and the blame are the same problem.

answers.q: What did you and the other designer disagree about?
answers.a: We disagreed about how faithful to be to the parent design system. The other senior designer wanted strict fidelity. I argued the system was built for web and did not survive the platform change: buttons were wrong as tap targets, type was not scaled, and the colors pulled too dark on a phone. I won on the interactive components and lost the rest. It is the same argument I would later lose at Sysgit, literal correctness against contextual fit.

source.label: Gradescope Mobile, Working as a pair

answers.q: What did you learn from it?
answers.a: The threshold for drop off is a totally different animal when nobody has to use your product. No one was required to use this app, so it had to demonstrate value over a process involving multiple apps. Every other product I have worked on had captive enterprise users. That distinction is the whole thing.

answers.q: Do you actually read documentation?
answers.a: Read it, yes. Write it, historically no. It is the thing I am worst at and it has a real cost, because far too much lives in my head. This site is the largest piece of documentation I have ever produced about my own work, which should tell you how overdue it was.

answers.q: Can I see your Figma files?
aliases: can i see the work files
can i see your work files
answers.a: Some of them, and fewer than you would expect. Most of my recent work happens in code, so the honest artifact is a pull request rather than a file full of frames. What survives from Turnitin and Slingshot I can walk you through. What I would rather show you is the running thing.

answers.q: What is your favorite color?
answers.a: #244233. Hue 150, saturation 30, lightness 20. The hue is the whole argument: 150 sits just off pure green toward blue, which is why it reads as pine rather than lawn. Real needles carry a waxy cuticle that scatters cool light, so they run colder than almost any other foliage. Saturation stays low because needles are never vivid, and lightness stays down because pine is a color you see in mass, not in a single leaf. Nearest ink is Pantone 5605 C.

answers.q: What is with the jackalope?
answers.a: Jackalopes are a cryptid 'native' to the State of Wyoming, just like me.

answers.q: What do you do when you are not designing?
aliases: what do you do for fun
what do you do on weekends
answers.a: I touch grass.

answers.q: Are you available?
answers.a: I am currently available for new projects.

answers.q: Where are you based, and will you relocate?
answers.a: I live in the Bay Area, specifically Oakland, PST. Would love a hybrid role but willing to work remote.

answers.q: What are your salary expectations?
answers.a: Let's just say that my expectations align with the fact that I am very good at what I do, I am a senior strategy player, and I live in the most expensive area in the country.

answers.q: What is the worst thing happening in design right now?
answers.a: Forced AI chatbots 😏.

answers.q: How do you work with engineers?
aliases: how do you hand off to engineering
what is your relationship with eng
do you work closely with builders
answers.a: Well, I'm basically an engineer now. But especially in a remote setting, I make sure there is always some form of kickoff and sanity check. I'm not just throwing designs over the fence. I also don't make builders wait on me for a fully fleshed design. We use the material of code and code reviews to communicate across different stages of the process.

answers.q: How do you align stakeholders who disagree?
aliases: how do you get people to agree
answers.a: The goal is to make sure everyone feels that their perspective is heard. Most of the time this means literally just making a space and time. It also helps to have a strong, data-backed product arm to refer to and lead the primary direction.

answers.q: How do you give difficult feedback?
aliases: how do you critique someone's work
delivering bad news to a designer
answers.a: Just say it. I tell the person I understand the parameters they previously operated under, and how we can both work toward a better outcome.

answers.q: How do you handle a PM who hands you solutions?
aliases: what if product hands you a solution
how do you push back on product
answers.a: Sometimes it's a non-issue. I always ask them to walk me through the problems they were trying to solve and how they came to those solutions. I treat it as an opportunity to collaborate rather than marching orders.

answers.q: What is an opinion you hold that others disagree with?
aliases: what do you believe that others do not
answers.a: Design is a human-centered practice. Art is not.

answers.q: How do you decide what to build first?
aliases: where do you start on a roadmap
answers.a: What will move the needle most. This can be anything from low-hanging fruit to tackling the hardest workflow first, based on the situation and stakeholder factors.

answers.q: How do you prioritize competing requests?
answers.a: Where did the request come from and who is making it. I recommend product designers get a foot in the door of revops, because that's where a lot of decisions are being made.

answers.q: How do you scope a project under a deadline?
aliases: what if there is not enough time
answers.a: I know the limits of my process and what the rest of my team needs. It's not just about establishing an MVP. When things are tight, I provide a menu of what I know I can do and make it the requester's decision.

answers.q: How do you know when a design is done?
aliases: how do you know to stop designing
answers.a: The cheeky answer is never. But I know when the remaining questions are ones I won't be able to answer until the prototype or build is released into the wild for feedback.

answers.q: How do you handle ambiguity?
aliases: what if the problem is not defined
how do you start when nothing is clear
answers.a: It is always easier to react to something that exists than to a series of possibilities. In an ambiguous situation I pick a lane, and open the floor up to what I got right and what I got wrong. Preferably sooner than later.

answers.q: What is your approach to design systems?
aliases: how do you build a design system
do you start a design system from scratch
answers.a: I am very rarely reinventing the wheel. A good starting point is finding a gold standard design system that is solving a similar issue, and then moulding it to fit the very specific needs and identity of the product. And always build in accessibility earlier than later.

answers.q: Have you built a component library?
aliases: have you built components in figma and code
answers.a: Yes. I have built entirely bespoke component systems bridging Figma, Storybook, and React components. But more commonly, and much more challenging, I have had to audit and revamp existing libraries, fix component creep, and pivot when an underlying technology disappears (please keep Tailwind in business 🙏).

answers.q: How do you think about accessibility?
aliases: is accessibility part of your process
answers.a: There are so many tools now to bake in accessibility as quickly as possible. Part of curbing scope is knowing what is pretty easy to get in first, like color visibility and ARIA, versus what actually requires judicious knowledge of the intended industry and users.

answers.q: Do you write specs?
aliases: do you write documentation for handoff
answers.a: Yes, depending on the scope of the work. For large concepts and initiatives, I typically keep a living document in Figma or, anymore, Claude that combines annotated screens with the overarching goals of the project, edge cases, and questions left unanswered. For smaller projects, the spec is a draft pull request, highlighting more minute changes, goals, and testing instructions to discover edge cases.

answers.q: How do you document your work?
answers.a: This answer seems to change every week. For large projects and concepts, I still like to bundle design specs with annotated screens in Figma files. I keep PRDs in a shared Claude project. Many of my designs I implement myself, and document in the code itself and in pull requests.

answers.q: How do you validate an idea cheaply?
aliases: how do you test an idea fast
answers.a: Believe it or not, I will still sketch on paper and snap photos of it. But for bigger product questions, or questions about interactions, AI is my new best friend. I can ideate three or four different interactive prototypes in Claude Design and send them to stakeholders to get clickthrough reactions within a few hours. Similarly, I can set up code sandboxes of prototypes that also reveal some of the technical cost of my ideas.

answers.q: What happens after launch?
aliases: what do you do once it ships
how do you follow up after release
answers.a: Feedback, feedback, followup. I never fall into the trap that anything launched is ever done. What users fixate on and report dictates the next step of work. I am part of weekly customer check-ins, and my Product Designer agent scrubs all feedback from in-app customer experience widgets, emails, and Slack.

answers.q: Have you designed for complex data?
aliases: have you worked on data heavy products
answers.a: Sure. Did you know there are over 32,105 actively monitored objects in earth's orbit right now? I designed a platform that relied on advanced astrodynamics to notify and arbitrate if one of your objects was about to hit any of the other 32,104.

answers.q: How do you design for uncertainty in model output?
aliases: how do you show model confidence
answers.a: The most important thing is to make the uncertainty very explicit, both in the language used, like "hmmm I'm not sure," and in the interaction, like intentionally displaying cycling or greying out unsure answers. Also surface anything the user can easily do to reduce the uncertainty, like follow-up questions or a request to rewrite the prompt.

answers.q: What does staff level mean to you?
answers.a: This is someone who is primarily an IC, who creates designs and artifacts, but on a systems scale rather than an individual team or feature. They own product strategy and vision, and design outputs on a level that is adopted by all product teams.

answers.q: What would you do in your first ninety days?
aliases: what would you do when you join
how would you start in a new role
answers.a: First is discovering the existing process and uncovering the gaps: how feedback is gathered, what the product strategy is, who decides what is built, and where the breakdowns are. That looks like bringing teams together and defining what a successful product looks like. Then an actual design audit: design systems, what is being built, and whether it matches the product goals.

answers.q: Do you prefer zero to one or scaling?
answers.a: As a dreamer, and someone who asks forgiveness not permission, I'll admit zero to one is more exciting.

answers.q: Are you more of a systems thinker or a craft person?
aliases: do you care more about structure or polish
answers.a: I would say I am a professional systems thinker with a craft hobby. I primarily want to solve problems, but I will talk at length about my favorite fonts.

answers.q: What is your ideal team structure?
aliases: what team do you work best in
who do you want to work with
answers.a: I work best on relatively small, independent teams. A few engineers, a few other designers, and ideally a very capable product person. I work best where everyone feels like they have product ownership and aren't afraid to try some weird things.

answers.q: Why design instead of engineering?
answers.a: Have you been talking to my immigrant parents? Seriously, pragmatically, I am both. I have always primarily been a visual and experiential person. I have a liberal arts background, but my entire career has been in tech working with complex systems. Even with AI, design is still the language of the masses, and the world needs more communicators than coders.

answers.q: How many years of experience do you have?
aliases: how long have you been designing
answers.a: I have 8 years of UX and product design experience, and over a decade working in product roles.

answers.q: What is your visual design strength?
aliases: what are you best at visually
what do you do better than other designers
answers.a: Information architecture. I make a hell of a table.

answers.q: Do you do motion design?
answers.a: Yes! I love a Bezier curve.

answers.q: Can you do branding?
answers.a: I can, but admittedly it's not my favorite.

answers.q: How much writing do you do?
aliases: is writing part of your practice
answers.a: Anymore my assistant Claude does a lot of the writing. I write enough to get the point across.

answers.q: Where do you find inspiration?
aliases: where do your ideas come from
answers.a: Nature, physical interfaces. I also play a lot of video games.

answers.q: How do you keep up with the field?
answers.a: There will always be thought leaders on the future of design, but honestly a lot of it is staying curious and playing with new products.

answers.q: What was Originality?
answers.a: Turnitin is primarily an academic integrity product. It is best known for its anti-plagiarism platform, but I worked on a lesser known issue: students buying papers from essay mills online. That was a slightly different problem, because the work was technically unique, just not by the student it was assigned to. The entire suite of academic integrity products was Originality. This has almost certainly changed since the AI boom.

answers.q: What was Gradescope Mobile?
answers.a: Gradescope is an automated grading tool that was acquired by Turnitin. At the time there was no clean way for students to digitize physical assignments for grading on the platform, so we created an app that allowed scanning and automated grading.

answers.q: How did teachers use it?
answers.a: Originality is basically a series of reports generated when a student submits a written assignment online. Teachers then use the scores and flags to determine if a student may have cheated.

answers.q: What is Sysgit?
answers.a: Systems engineering plus Git. It is a tool for hardware modeling and requirements management that uses existing Git principles for version control.
